lesson.title: Empirical Analysis: Timing Your Code Instead of Just Predicting It
lesson.summary: Empirical analysis measures an algorithm's actual running time on real inputs, using timed experiments to check, support, or challenge the Big-O predictions made through mathematical analysis.
lesson.body:
Everything in this unit so far has been theoretical analysis: reading code and reasoning about how its operation count should grow. Empirical analysis is the complementary skill of actually running code and measuring what happens, the same instinct behind Testing, where you run code against real cases to check that your reasoning about it was correct.

Python's standard library makes basic timing straightforward with the time module.

import time

def time_function(func, *args):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    func(*args)
    end = time.perf_counter()
    return end - start

values_1k = list(range(1000))
values_10k = list(range(10000))

t1 = time_function(sum_all, values_1k)
t2 = time_function(sum_all, values_10k)
print(t1, t2)

If sum_all is genuinely O(n), you would expect t2 to be roughly 10 times t1, since values_10k is 10 times larger than values_1k. Running this kind of experiment across several increasing input sizes, then looking at how the measured times scale, is the core technique of empirical analysis.

A good empirical test does not just compare two sizes, it tests a range and looks at the pattern. If you time an algorithm on inputs of size 1,000, 2,000, 4,000, and 8,000, each double the last, the same doubling thought experiment used throughout this unit, now applied with a stopwatch instead of a pencil, you can compare the ratios of consecutive times. Roughly constant ratios close to 2 suggest O(n). Ratios close to 4 suggest O(n^2), since doubling n should roughly quadruple n^2. Ratios only slightly above 1 suggest O(log n). This lets you infer an algorithm's time complexity from measurements alone, without reading or fully understanding its code.

Empirical analysis is valuable precisely because theoretical Big-O analysis can miss real world effects. Constant factors that Big-O deliberately ignores can matter enormously in practice: an O(n) algorithm with a large constant factor can be slower than an O(n log n) algorithm on realistic input sizes, even though the O(n) algorithm would eventually win for large enough n. Hardware effects like cache behavior, memory allocation, and how a specific language implementation optimizes loops can also cause real timings to diverge from the clean predictions of counting operations on paper.

The two approaches work best together, not as substitutes for each other. Theoretical analysis, counting operations and reasoning about worst case, gives you guarantees that hold for any input size, including sizes you have not tested yet. Empirical analysis, timing real runs, tells you what is actually happening on your machine, with your data, at the sizes you care about right now, and can catch mistakes in your theoretical reasoning, like an accidentally quadratic piece of code you assumed was linear. A careful programmer uses Big-O to predict behavior and empirical testing to confirm it.
